En [[al-matrices|el tema de matrices]] l: In [[al-matrices|the topic on matrices]] you saw them as tables of numbers. There is a far more illuminating way of understanding them: a matrix is a transformation of space. It takes the whole plane, stretches it, compresses it, rotates it and shears it, all at once.

Esto tiene una consecuencia práctica eno: This has an enormous practical consequence. Computing $A^{100}$ by multiplying a hundred times is unworkable; but $A^{100} = P D^{100} P^{-1}$, and raising a diagonal matrix to a power is raising its entries one by one. That is how Markov chains, the evolution of age-structured populations and linear dynamical systems are solved.
Y tiene una consecuencia menos amable. S: And it has a less friendly consequence. If $|\lambda| < 1$, then $\lambda^{100}$ is practically zero, and if $|\lambda| > 1$ it is enormous: raising to a large power crushes or blows up, with almost no middle ground. That is exactly what happens to a network applied to itself many times, and the reason why long dependencies could not be learned for years. It is in [[ia-recurrentes|networks with memory]].

El algoritmo PageRank, con el que Google: The PageRank algorithm, with which Google ordered the web in 1998, is essentially this: an enormous matrix is built from the links between pages and its principal eigenvector is sought. The importance of each page is its component in that eigenvector. A doctoral thesis, an eigenvector and a trillion-dollar company.
Hay un caso en el que la matriz cuyos au: There is a case in which the matrix whose eigenvectors are sought is manufactured by the data themselves. If you take a cloud of points and build the matrix recording how much each variable varies and how much they go together, its eigenvectors turn out to be the directions in which the cloud stretches most, and each eigenvalue measures exactly how much. That is [[av-pca|principal component analysis]], and it is the most widespread way of summarising data of many variables in a few numbers.
Los autovectores de una nube de datos: The eigenvectors of a cloud of data
Los autovalores son las frecuencias prop: Eigenvalues are the natural frequencies of a structure, and knowing them is a matter of safety. A bridge, a skyscraper or an aircraft wing vibrates naturally at certain frequencies, and if an outside excitation matches one of them, the amplitude grows on its own: that is resonance. London's Millennium Bridge had to close two days after opening in the year 2000 because people walking excited one of its natural modes. Computing eigenvalues is what prevents that.
Hay matrices que no dejan ninguna direcc: There are matrices that leave no direction untwisted. The most obvious is a rotation: if the whole plane turns $90^\circ$, no vector ends up on its own line, and the characteristic equation has no real roots. But it does have [[al-complejos|complex]] roots, and those roots say exactly how much the transformation rotates and how much it stretches.

The characteristic equation is $(a - \lambda)^2 + b^2 = 0$, so $\lambda = a \pm bi$.

The modulus of the eigenvalue, $r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, is how much the matrix stretches; its argument, $\theta$, how much it rotates.

Multiplying the vector $(x, y)$ by $A$ gives the same as multiplying the complex number $x + yi$ by $a + bi$: complex numbers are rotations with scaling.
Toda matriz real 2×2 con autovalores com: Every real 2×2 matrix with complex eigenvalues $a \pm bi$ behaves like this in a suitable basis: at each application it rotates by an angle $\theta$ and stretches by $r$. If $r < 1$, the points spiral in towards the origin; if $r > 1$, they spiral away; if $r = 1$, they turn for ever on a closed curve. It is the same stability criterion as for [[av-sistemas-dinamicos|dynamical systems]].
Se aplica la matriz una y otra vez a un: The matrix is applied again and again to a starting point. Each application rotates by an angle θ and stretches by r, the two data of the complex eigenvalue. Set r exactly at 1 and the point goes round without approaching or receding.
